title: Kafka / Messaging / Event-Driven Architecture
primer: Kafka answers center on consumer groups, lag, and delivery semantics: at-least-once is the default, so consumers must be idempotent and commit offsets after side effects succeed. Partition keys buy ordering and can buy skew. Poison messages need bounded retries and a DLQ. Prefer an outbox when DB state and events must stay aligned, and choose Kafka only when fan-out, replay, or high throughput justify it.

cheatStrip.v: commit after DB success (or transactional outbox)
retry budget → DLQ, don't block partition forever

quiz.q: Kafka consumer groups scale parallelism primarily by:

options.t: Number of partitions (one consumer per partition per group)

quiz.explain: Within a group, each partition is consumed by at most one consumer; more consumers than partitions sit idle.

quiz.q: Safer offset policy when writing to Postgres:

options.t: Commit offset after the DB transaction succeeds
Commit offset before processing to maximize throughput

quiz.explain: Commit-after-success yields at-least-once with possible duplicates; commit-before risks data loss.

options.t: One key hashes to a hot partition and overloads it
All partitions always have identical lag

quiz.explain: Popular keys concentrate load; consumers on cold partitions stay underutilized.

options.t: Dual-write races between DB commit and Kafka publish

quiz.explain: Write row + outbox row atomically; a publisher relays outbox events to Kafka.

questions.question: A Kafka consumer is processing messages slower than producers are publishing them. How would you diagnose and scale it?
questions.first30s: I'd check consumer group lag by partition, see whether we're CPU-bound in processing or blocked on I/O, then scale partitions/consumers or speed up the handler — lag is the north star.
modelAnswer: Measure lag (records/time) per partition and consumer; confirm it's growing, not a transient spike.
Profile the handler: DB, external HTTP, serialization, batch size, sync vs async commits.
Scale horizontally: increase partitions (plan carefully) so more consumers in the group can share work; adding consumers beyond partition count doesn't help.
Optimize: batch writes, pipelining, reduce per-message DB round-trips, parallelize only where ordering allows.
If one partition lags, suspect key skew; fix keying or processing isolation for whales.
questions.sayIt: Lag tells me I'm falling behind. I find whether it's handler time or skew, then add partitions/consumers or make each message cheaper.
questions.nestNote: Expose lag metrics to Prometheus from the consumer client or burrow-like monitor.
traps: Adding consumers without adding partitions
Auto-scaling consumers blindly on CPU while lag is key-skew
Raising fetch sizes without measuring GC/DB impact
followUps: How do you choose the initial partition count?
What's the cost of increasing partitions later?

questions.question: A consumer processes the same event twice. How should the application handle duplicates?
questions.first30s: Treat duplicates as normal under at-least-once. Make processing idempotent with a dedupe key stored where the side effect lives.
modelAnswer: Assume at-least-once: rebalances, retries, and commit failures cause redelivery.
Define an idempotency key (event id, orderId+type, producer UUID) unique per business effect.
Persist processed keys in Postgres (unique constraint) in the same transaction as the side effect.
For non-DB effects, use Redis SET NX with TTL or upstream idempotent APIs.
Don't 'fix' duplicates by committing offsets earlier — that risks loss.
questions.sayIt: Duplicates are expected. I key every side effect and upsert under a unique constraint so the second delivery is a no-op.
traps: Assuming Kafka exactly-once means the business effect is exactly-once without work
Dedupe in memory only (lost on restart)
Side effects outside the dedupe transaction
followUps: How does Kafka EOS / transactions change this?
How long do you retain idempotency keys?

questions.question: A consumer updates PostgreSQL and crashes before committing its Kafka offset. What could happen?
questions.first30s: On restart the message is redelivered. If the DB write already committed, you get a duplicate side effect unless the consumer is idempotent.
modelAnswer: Crash after DB commit + before offset commit ⇒ redelivery ⇒ duplicate processing attempt.
Crash before DB commit ⇒ redelivery replays safely if the first write never landed.
This is why commit-after-success + idempotent writes is the standard pattern.
Opposite anti-pattern: commit offset first ⇒ crash ⇒ message skipped ⇒ data loss.
Operationally: expect rebalances to extend this window; design for it, don't treat it as rare.
questions.sayIt: DB committed, offset not: redelivery. That's at-least-once — idempotency makes it safe; committing early makes loss possible.
questions.nestNote: Enable graceful shutdown that finishes the current record and commits before exit when possible.
traps: Believing 'we commit sync so duplicates can't happen'
Committing offsets in a finally block before knowing DB success
No unique constraints on the write path
followUps: How do store-offset-in-DB patterns work?
What happens during a rebalance mid-processing?

questions.question: How would you design an idempotent Kafka consumer?
questions.first30s: Stable event id, transactional side effect + dedupe record, commit offsets only after success, and bounded retries for poison messages.
modelAnswer: Require producers to send a unique eventId (or derive a deterministic hash of natural key + revision).
In one DB transaction: insert dedupe row (unique on eventId) + apply business writes; skip if conflict.
Keep handlers pure regarding retries: no non-idempotent external calls without their own idempotency keys.
Commit Kafka offsets only after the transaction succeeds (or write offsets into the DB transaction).
On repeated failure after N tries, route to DLQ and commit/skip so the partition progresses.
questions.sayIt: Idempotent consumer = unique event id + transactional dedupe with the side effect + offset commit after success + DLQ for poison.
questions.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A[Poll] --> B{eventId seen?}
  B -->|yes| C[Skip / commit]
  B -->|no| D[TX: side effect + mark seen]
  D --> E[Commit offset]
questions.nestNote: Nest/KafkaJS: disable auto-commit or commit explicitly after business TX.
traps: Idempotency key that's not unique across retries (e.g. random UUID generated in consumer)
External payment call inside handler without provider idempotency key
Infinite retry blocking the partition
followUps: How do you idempotently call a third-party API from a consumer?

questions.question: How would you choose a Kafka partition key for an order or user domain?
questions.first30s: Pick a key that preserves the ordering you need and spreads load — usually orderId for order lifecycle, userId for per-user streams — and watch for hot keys.
modelAnswer: Ordering is per partition: all events for one orderId on the same partition keep causal order for that order.
Use orderId when order state machine ordering matters; userId when per-user sequencing matters (feeds, balances).
Avoid null/empty keys if you need ordering; avoid a single global key that serializes the topic.
Balance cardinality: enough distinct keys to utilize partitions; monitor hotspot users/orders.
Document the key so producers stay consistent — mixed keys destroy ordering assumptions.
questions.sayIt: Partition key = ordering scope. orderId for order timelines, userId for user timelines — never one key for the whole topic.
questions.code: producer.send({ topic: 'orders', key: orderId, value: event })
traps: Random keys when you needed per-entity ordering
Using a low-cardinality status field as key
Changing key mid-stream without a migration plan
followUps: How do you order across multiple entity types?
What if a single userId is too hot?

questions.question: One Kafka partition is receiving much more traffic than the others. How would you diagnose and fix the imbalance?
questions.first30s: That's key skew. I'd measure produce rates per partition, find the hot keys, then re-key, split whales, or add processing isolation — more consumers alone won't fix one hot partition.
modelAnswer: Confirm with broker/partition metrics: bytes-in, message rate, consumer lag on one partition.
Sample keys in the hot partition; identify celebrity userId/orderId or bad constant key.
Fixes: choose a higher-cardinality key; salt hot keys (trade ordering); split entity processing; dedicated topic for whales.
Increasing partitions helps new keys redistribute but won't split an existing hot key's stream without changing the key.
Long-term: producer guidelines + dashboards for partition imbalance.
questions.sayIt: Hot partition is key skew. Find the key, change keying or isolate the whale — extra consumers can't share one partition.
traps: Scaling consumer count expecting the hot partition to split
Salting keys without accepting lost per-key order
Ignoring producer-side constant keys
followUps: How does sticky partitioning interact with skew?
Can you manually reassign partitions to stronger consumers?

questions.question: How would you design retries without allowing one poison message to block unrelated processing?
questions.first30s: Bounded retries with backoff, then DLQ — never infinite retry on the same record while holding up the partition.
modelAnswer: Classify errors: transient (retry) vs permanent/poison (don't tight-loop).
Retry with backoff and a max attempts counter (headers or side store).
After budget: publish to DLQ/retry topic with reason/payload; commit/skip the original so the partition advances.
Process DLQ asynchronously with alerting and replay tools; don't require on-call to unblock the main topic.
Where ordering allows, use pause/seek carefully; prefer per-record isolation over stopping the whole consumer.
questions.sayIt: Retry transient errors with a budget, then DLQ and move on — one bad message must not stall the partition.
questions.nestNote: KafkaJS eachMessage handlers should not throw endlessly without a DLQ path.
traps: Infinite retries on deserialization errors
Blocking the consumer thread on long sleeps
DLQ without alerts or replay procedure
followUps: Retry topic vs in-place retry — trade-offs?
How do you preserve ordering when skipping poison pills?

questions.question: When would you choose Kafka versus SQS, RabbitMQ, or a synchronous API call?
questions.first30s: Sync API for request/response latency paths. SQS for simple durable queues on AWS. Rabbit for flexible routing/work queues. Kafka for high-throughput event logs, replay, and many independent consumers.
modelAnswer: Synchronous HTTP/gRPC when the caller needs an immediate answer and the work is short.
SQS: managed queue, at-least-once, easy workers, limited fan-out/replay story — great for job queues.
RabbitMQ: routing keys, competing consumers, classic work-queue patterns; not an infinite retained log by default.
Kafka: durable partitioned log, consumer groups, replay from offsets, high throughput event streaming and fan-out.
Don't use Kafka as a RPC substitute; don't use sync HTTP for bursty fan-out work that can be async.
questions.sayIt: Sync for immediate answers, SQS/Rabbit for work queues, Kafka when I need a replayable event log and independent consumer groups at scale.
traps: Using Kafka for every tiny async job
Using sync calls for multi-minute workflows
Assuming SQS gives the same replay model as Kafka

questions.question: How would you evolve an event schema without breaking existing consumers?
questions.first30s: Prefer additive, backward-compatible changes with a schema registry — consumers must tolerate new fields; removals need a coordinated expand-contract.
modelAnswer: Use Avro/Protobuf/JSON Schema with a registry and compatibility mode (BACKWARD/FORWARD/FULL) enforced in CI.
Safe changes: add optional fields with defaults; avoid renaming/removing/changing types without a version plan.
Expand-contract: publish both old and new fields, upgrade consumers, then drop old fields.
Include eventType + schemaVersion in envelopes; don't overload one event name with incompatible meanings.
Test consumers against new schemas in pipeline; canary producers first.
questions.sayIt: Additive evolution under registry compatibility rules. Breaking changes take expand-contract and versioned event types — never silent field deletes.
traps: Renaming fields in place
No compatibility checks in CI
Reusing event names for different semantics
followUps: FORWARD vs BACKWARD compatibility — who upgrades first?
How do you handle poisoned messages with unknown schema versions?

questions.question: How would you use the outbox pattern to keep database state and published events consistent?
questions.first30s: In the same Postgres transaction as the business write, insert an outbox row; a separate publisher drains the outbox to Kafka so you never dual-write across two systems unsafely.
modelAnswer: Problem: commit DB then fail to publish (or vice versa) ⇒ inconsistency.
Solution: BEGIN; business rows + INSERT outbox(event); COMMIT.
Publisher polls outbox (or CDC) and produces to Kafka; mark published / delete with idempotent produce.
Consumers remain idempotent; outbox publisher must handle retries without dup chaos (idempotent produce keys).
Observe lag between outbox insert and Kafka publish; alert on stuck rows.
questions.sayIt: Outbox: one DB transaction for state + event row, async relay to Kafka. No dual-write hope.
questions.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  App->>Postgres: TX business + outbox
  Publisher->>Postgres: read outbox
  Publisher->>Kafka: produce
  Publisher->>Postgres: mark published
questions.nestNote: Implement outbox publisher as a Nest worker; keep HTTP handlers free of Kafka produce retries.
traps: Publishing to Kafka inside the request without an outbox
Deleting outbox rows before Kafka ack
No metrics on outbox depth
followUps: Polling vs Debezium CDC for outbox?
How do you ensure exactly-once produce from the publisher?
